sections.content: *Que* and *de que* both open a clause, and the choice depends on the word before them. A verb, noun or adjective that takes *de* keeps it: *me alegro de eso*, so *me alegro de que…*. One that takes no *de* never gets one: *pienso eso*, so *pienso que…*. To check, replace the clause with *eso* and see whether *de* belongs. Adding an unwanted *de* (*pienso de que…*) is *dequeísmo*; dropping a needed one (*me alegro que…*) is *queísmo*. Both are frequent in speech, and both count as errors in formal writing, so an editor corrects them.

sections.title: The eso test
rows: Opino que el texto es claro.
I think the text is clear. (opino eso: no de)
I think there is a mistake. (creo eso: no de)
Me alegro de que lo corrijan.
I am glad they are correcting it. (me alegro de eso: de)
Me di cuenta de que había una errata.
I realised there was a misprint. (me di cuenta de eso: de)
Estoy seguro de que es correcto.
I am sure it is correct. (estoy seguro de eso: de)
Rechazo la idea de que una errata no importa.
I reject the idea that a misprint does not matter. (la idea de eso: de)

sections.content: English *that* gives no clue: 'I think that…' and 'I am glad that…' look alike. Learn the verb with its preposition as one unit (*alegrarse de*, *darse cuenta de*) and use the *eso* test when unsure. Watch the pairs that mean the same but differ: *me acuerdo de que…* but *recuerdo que…*.
